# Process cooling water cleaning, flushing and passivation — Tull Creek Data Hall, turnover package

You are the commissioning engineer for the flushing contractor on a new data hall. The project
document library for this task is the directory tree around this file: `drawings/` (P&ID and
isometric sheets, site logistics and the temporary power single line, DXF, plan units are feet),
`schedules/` (pipe, equipment, valve and tie-in schedules, XLSX), `specs/` (the project
specification sections, DOCX), `standards/` (the public standards and criteria documents the
specification adopts, PDF), `site/` (construction water, the water analysis, the discharge
authorisation and temporary power, DOCX / PDF / XLSX), `vendor_data/` (reviewed submittals and a
priced chemical quotation, PDF / XLSX), `commissioning/` (turnover milestones, the hydrostatic test
record and a checklist template, XLSX / CSV) and `correspondence/` (RFI responses). Not every
document is relevant, and the information you need is spread across them: read the project
specification first and let it tell you which documents govern what.

Some documents in the library are **scanned images with no text layer**. Their contents cannot be
extracted as text and must be read as images; do not conclude that a document is empty or
irrelevant because text extraction returns nothing.

## Situation

The Process Cooling Water (PCW) loop is mechanically complete. It is divided into eight
tie-in-bounded circuits of different sizes, metallurgies and hold-up volumes. Before turnover every
circuit must be flushed, chemically cleaned, rinsed, passivated and filled with its treatment
programme, and the whole campaign must be executed with a fixed rented fleet of flush skids, a
metered construction-water allocation, a single authorised sewer discharge point, the temporary
power available at each tie-in, two commissioning crews and a contractual turnover date.

Which lines belong to which circuit is shown on the drawings, not tabulated anywhere. The rest of
the engineering is yours: the flow each circuit must be flushed at and whether the skid you assign
can deliver it against that circuit's head; the treatment programme each circuit's metallurgy and
the site's makeup water admit; how much product that needs and how long the passivation film must be
held; how many rinse displacements it takes to reach the acceptance criterion; whether rinse water
can be cascaded from one circuit to another; where each discharge goes; and how all of that fits the
water, fleet, power, discharge and schedule limits at the lowest total programme cost.

## Deliverable

Produce `output/submission.zip` containing the seven files below. **The schema is a contract, not
part of the problem: every column and every stage token you need is listed here.** Column names are
matched case-insensitively and `_`, `-` and space are equivalent; common synonyms are accepted, and
extra columns of your own are ignored. Rows may be in any order. Use these stage tokens:

    HYDRO   INITIAL_FLUSH   CHEM_CLEAN   DRAIN_RINSE   PASSIVATE   HOLD   FINAL_FILL

You may add activities of your own (set-up, strainer removal, demobilisation); they are ignored, not
penalised. A stage token that cannot be resolved costs the package family; and if the stage it was
meant to be was one of the seven above, the circuit also loses every family that needed that stage —
an unreadable token does not stand in for the stage it was meant to name.

One cell value is fatal, and only in one place. In the numeric columns the grader reads — `flow_gpm`,
`velocity_fps`, `reynolds`, `required_head_ft`, `skid_head_avail_ft`, `duration_h`,
`circuit_volume_gal`, `system_volume_gal`, `passes`, `water_volume_gal`, `discharge_volume_gal`,
`discharge_ph`, `discharge_temp_f`, `target_ppm`, `product_quantity`, `basis_volume_gal`,
`ph_target_lo`, `ph_target_hi`, `threshold_value`, `start_h`, `finish_h` — a cell reading `TBD`,
`TBA`, `to be determined`, `to be advised`, `NaN`, `Inf`, `XXX` or `<fill in>` scores the whole
package zero: a placeholder
is not an answer — in any of the four plan CSVs, on any row. In any other column, including every
column of your own, those words are ignored. `--`, `N/A`, `NONE` and an empty cell are ordinary
"not applicable" everywhere and are never penalised, so a column a row does not use (the skid and
flow columns on `HYDRO` and `HOLD`, the test pressure off the hydrostatic row) should be left blank
or set to one of those rather than to `TBD`.

The rented fleet is a closed vocabulary: `skid_id` on a pumped row must name one or more of the
three units on hire, `+`-joined. Case, spaces, hyphens and underscores are equivalent. A cell that
names anything else — a model rather than a unit, a unit that was never hired, or nothing at all —
costs the skid-fleet family for the programme; it never makes the package unreadable.

`HYDRO` and `HOLD` are not pumped stages: on those rows the skid, flow, velocity, Reynolds and head
columns do not apply and may be left blank or set to `NONE`. `HYDRO` carries its test pressure and
its duration; `HOLD` carries only its duration. Every other stage carries the full row. A circuit
whose hydrostatic test is already on record as accepted needs no `HYDRO` row; if you file one for
it, give it a duration of zero and no water, and it is read as a test not performed.

1. `flush_plan.csv` — one row per circuit and stage. Columns:
   `circuit_id` · `stage` · `skid_id` (the rented unit ids, `+`-joined if more than one) ·
   `skids_parallel` (count) · `flow_gpm` · `governing_segment` (line number) ·
   `governing_id_in` (in.) · `velocity_fps` (ft/s) · `reynolds` · `required_head_ft` (ft w.c.) ·
   `skid_head_avail_ft` (ft w.c.) · `duration_h` (the scheduled occupancy, hours) ·
   `circuit_volume_gal` (the FLUSH volume) · `system_volume_gal` · `passes` (displacements, on the
   flush and rinse rows) · `water_source` (`MAKEUP`, or `CASCADE_FROM:<circuit>`) ·
   `water_volume_gal` · `discharge_route` (`SEWER`, `HAUL` or `NONE`) · `discharge_volume_gal` ·
   `discharge_ph` · `discharge_temp_f` (degF) · `test_pressure_psig` (on the hydrostatic row) ·
   `protection` (the temporary bypasses and strainer fitted for that stage) ·
   `turnover_method` (the method the project specification permits at turnover).
2. `chemistry_plan.csv` — one row per circuit, stage and product. Columns:
   `circuit_id` · `stage` · `program` (the treatment programme, on the treatment rows) ·
   `product_id` · `active_species` · `target_ppm` · `basis_volume_gal` (the volume the dose is
   referred to) · `product_quantity` · `product_unit` · `packages` (whole packages) ·
   `ph_target_lo` · `ph_target_hi` · `hold_days` · `source_doc` · `source_clause`.
   A roll-up row whose stage is an order total is ignored.
3. `acceptance_matrix.csv` — one row per circuit, gate and parameter. Columns:
   `circuit_id` · `gate` · `parameter` · `method` · `sample_point_tag` ·
   `threshold_op` (`>=`/`<=`, or `lower limit`/`upper limit`) · `threshold_value` · `units` ·
   `basis_doc` · `basis_clause`. The gates and parameters the turnover log must carry are listed in
   the project specification; the grader matches a row by its gate and the quantity named in its
   parameter, not by an exact spelling.
4. `schedule.csv` — one row per activity; a stage may be split into several. Columns:
   `activity_id` · `circuit_id` · `stage` · `predecessor_ids` · `start_h` · `finish_h` (hours from
   mobilisation) · `skid_id` · `crew_id` · `water_draw_gal`.
5. `resources.json` — an object with `skid_assignment`, `water_profile`, `discharge_profile`,
   `power_check`, `chemical_orders` and `cost`. `chemical_orders` is a list of objects carrying at
   least `product_id`, `packages`, `lead_days` and `order_by_day` (days from mobilisation; negative
   means before it). `cost` carries the breakdown and a total under `total_usd`.
6. `constraint_register.csv` — columns `id, document, clause, requirement, value, items_bound`:
   every requirement you applied, each with the document and clause or table it comes from, the
   value you used and what it binds. Cite the real project documents and clauses, not this brief.
   The register is scored on recall of the requirements the grader checks (at least 90 % of the hard
   requirements must be present, matched on document plus clause) and on value agreement; extra
   correct rows are neutral and there is no cap on the number of rows, and **a hard requirement
   missing from the register makes every family it governs count as not passed**. Rows citing a
   superseded, cancelled or non-adopted document as their authority count against you: **a single
   such row fails the register family**. Recording that a document is superseded while citing the
   current one, or citing a standard an adopted document itself invokes, is not such a row.
   **The register lists only the requirements you applied.** A row whose `document` cell names a
   superseded, cancelled or non-adopted document is a row citing that document as its authority
   **whatever its requirement or value text says** — writing "out of scope", "not applied" or
   "reviewed and rejected" in another column does not make it a different row. Record the documents
   you read and rejected, and why, in `MOP.md`, not in the register.
7. `MOP.md` — the Method of Procedure: the execution narrative **and** the design basis. The design
   basis must give, for each circuit, **the governing constraint and its margin**. The governing
   constraint is whichever of these five your own plan leaves the least room against — the flushing
   duty against the head the assigned skid can deliver; the rinse endpoint; the authorised programme
   discharge volume; the site's daily water allocation; the temporary power available at the tie-in
   — and the margin is the fractional room left, `(limit − achieved) / limit`, as a decimal. Name
   one per circuit and state its margin. Some of these margins can be written in more than one
   quantity — the rinse in displacements or in the quantity its endpoint is measured in — and they
   are genuinely different numbers; **every form the project specification permits counts, and which
   constraint binds is decided using whichever permitted form of each is the tighter**, so a
   constraint that is tightest in any permitted quantity is a defensible answer. The rinse margin may be
   given either in displacements or in whatever quantity the acceptance
   criterion you are working to is expressed in. Which one binds, and by how much, is yours to
   work out; record the resolution of every conflict you found between the
   project documents, the margins and judgement calls you made, the defects you found, and a safety
   section discharging the chemical-handling obligations of the standard the specification adopts
   for hazard communication.

Every number you report must agree with the plan it describes: the figures that are scored are
recomputed from your flows, passes, routes, methods and schedule, not taken from your columns.
The rinse is the one exception for the effluent columns: its effluent runs from the spent
cleaning solution to the makeup water over the displacements, so any `discharge_ph` and
`discharge_temp_f` inside the acceptance band the discharge authorisation states is accepted on
a `DRAIN_RINSE` row.

The project specification states how water, effluent, attended time and cost are accounted, and what
the turnover options are. Follow it: the plan is priced on that basis.

## How the package is assessed

The plan is checked circuit by circuit against the requirements of the project documents, and the
programme is credited for its total cost against the lowest cost the documents allow: a cheaper
programme scores higher. Each circuit scores 0.4·p + 0.6·[h = 1]·O, where p is the fraction of its 24
constraint families that count, h the fraction of its 20 hard families that count (a family counts
when the circuit passes it and the register carries the hard requirements that govern it; [h = 1] is
1 when all 20 count, else 0), and O is the lowest cost the documents allow divided by the cost of your
programme, at most 1. A hard failure withholds O. The task score is the mean over the graded circuits.
A circuit whose rows are missing or unparseable scores 0.

Work from the documents. Where they leave something to the engineer, decide and record it in the
design basis.


## Verifier access (blind variant)

No verifier, oracle, or evaluation data of any kind is available in this workspace — the
only checks you can run are the ones you build yourself. Work from the brief and the
documents alone and submit your best final deliverable; it will be graded offline by the
frozen verifier on held-out instances.

Tull Creek Data Hall - Engineer of Record response, 2026-06-26
Question (flush contractor): Schedule M-601 lists lines 6011, 6012 and 6013 as galvanized. Please confirm, as the remainder of the PCW system is black steel and copper.
Response: Confirmed. Lines 6011, 6012 and 6013, and the break tank ST-601, are hot-dip galvanized. They were specified galvanized for the makeup and fill duty and were installed as specified. No change is required.

1   METERED CONSTRUCTION WATER
The site construction water meter is limited by the utility agreement to 62,000 gallons in any calendar day, for all trades. For the duration of the PCW flushing scope the whole of that allocation is assigned to this scope.
Metered construction water is charged at $6.20 per 1,000 gallons.
2   TRUCKED WATER
Additional potable water may be trucked in, up to 30,000 gallons in any calendar day, at $19.80 per 1,000 gallons delivered. Trucked water is of the same analysis as the metered supply (SW-02).
THE LIMIT ON A DAY'S DRAW. Read the two paragraphs above together: the most water this scope may draw in any one calendar day is 92,000 gallons - the 62,000 gallon metered allocation PLUS the 30,000 gallon trucked entitlement. Drawing more than that in a day is not possible and no plan may schedule it. The metered allocation is NOT a limit on what may be drawn: it is where the PRICE changes. Volume above it in a day is bought at the trucked rate and is permitted, up to the trucked limit.
Water drawn by an activity that spans midnight is counted against each calendar day in proportion to the hours of the activity that fall in that day.
3   FLUSH EQUIPMENT
Three flush skids are AVAILABLE to this scope: two FS-600 units (FS-600-A, FS-600-B) and one FS-1200 unit (FS-1200-A). No further units are available, and no unit may serve two circuits at the same time.
Availability is not hire. A unit is on hire only on a calendar day on which it is HELD - that is, a day on which some scheduled activity declaring it overlaps - and it is charged its day rate once for each such day, whatever work it does that day. A unit that is not held on a day is not charged for that day, and no unit is charged for the duration of the scope merely because it is available to it. Section 23 25 16 cl.3.10 a states how a day's hire is divided between the circuits that shared it.
Commissioning crews are engaged by the shift, of 12 hours, at $820.00 per shift, and a shift in which a crew attends anything at all is charged whole. No more than 2 crews may be on the works at once.
A unit serves one circuit at a time and a crew attends one activity at a time; the cost basis of 23 25 16 cl.3.10 divides each unit-day and each crew-shift between the circuits that shared it.

SECTION 23 25 16 - PROCESS COOLING WATER CLEANING, FLUSHING AND PASSIVATION
Tull Creek Data Hall - Issued for Construction, Rev 3, 2026-07-14
1.1   SUMMARY
This Section covers pre-operational cleaning, flushing, chemical cleaning, passivation and turnover of the Process Cooling Water (PCW) system, circuit by circuit.
The PCW system is a closed process cooling water loop. Apply the closed-system provisions of the governing water-treatment criteria document; the provisions written for open recirculating cooling-tower systems do not apply to this system except where this Section invokes them explicitly.
Where this Section and the governing water-treatment criteria document both address a subject, the more restrictive requirement governs.
1.2   GOVERNING DOCUMENTS
UFC 3-230-13, Industrial Water Treatment Operation and Maintenance (current edition). The 2005 edition, UFC 3-240-13FN, is cancelled and must not be used.
DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92, Thermodynamics, Heat Transfer and Fluid Flow, Volume 3, for all hydraulic relations.
40 CFR 403, General Pretreatment Regulations, for discharge to the publicly owned treatment works.
29 CFR 1910.1200, Hazard Communication, for all products brought on site.
Section 23 21 16 for pipe materials, roughness and the hydrostatic test regime.
1.5   FLUSHING, TESTING AND WATER-TREATMENT LOG
Maintain and submit a log recording, for every circuit: the minimum flushing velocity achieved and the segment at which it was measured; the temporary strainer mesh and its removal milestone; the chemical cleaning circulation time; the rinse water test results (clarity, suspended solids, conductivity and pH) against the makeup water; the passivation inhibitor residual, pH and film-formation hold duration; and every discharge event with its volume, route, pH and temperature. Use the form of CX-03.
Submit with the log an acceptance matrix stating, for every circuit, the acceptance threshold applied at each gate, with the document and clause it comes from. The matrix must carry at least the following, each with the sense and the numeric value of its threshold:
  a. RINSE gate: conductivity (upper limit), pH (lower limit and upper limit);
  b. PASSIVATION gate: the inhibitor residual at the start of film formation (lower limit);
  c. DISCHARGE gate: pH (lower limit) and temperature (upper limit) at the authorised discharge point;
  d. TURNOVER gate: the maintenance inhibitor residual (lower limit) and the total aerobic bacteria count (upper limit), both to the limits of the governing water-treatment criteria document.
1.6   DESIGN BASIS AND METHOD OF PROCEDURE
Submit a Method of Procedure (MOP) containing the execution narrative and the design basis.
Where a constraint can be expressed in more than one quantity - the rinse, for instance, in displacements or in conductivity - the margin may be stated in ANY of them; state which.
The design basis must state, for each circuit, a line of exactly the form
    GOVERNING CONSTRAINT <circuit>: <constraint family> (margin <value>)
where <constraint family> is the constraint family that is binding for that circuit and <value> is its relative margin, that is (limit - achieved)/limit for an upper limit and (achieved - limit)/limit for a lower limit, as a decimal fraction.
The design basis must also record the resolution of every conflict found between the project documents, the margins applied, and the defects found in the documents.
3.2   HYDRAULIC BASIS
Compute every hydraulic quantity by the relations of DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92 with the following project conventions. Design flush water properties: density 62.30 lbm/ft3, kinematic viscosity 1.08e-5 ft2/s at 68 degF.
For DOSING arithmetic - converting a target residual in parts per million to a mass of active species - use a water density of 8.34 lb/gal. A residual of 1 ppm in 1,000 gallons is therefore 0.00834 lb of the active species.
a. Velocity in a leg is v = Q_leg / A, where Q_leg is that leg's share of the circuit flow and A is the inside cross-sectional area from Schedule M-601. Parallel legs of one line carry an equal share.
b. Friction factor from the Colebrook-White relation, solved iteratively:
       1/sqrt(f) = -2 log10( (e/D)/3.7 + 2.51/(Re sqrt(f)) )
   with absolute roughness e from Section 23 21 16 and Re = v D / nu. Below Re 2000 use f = 64/Re.
c. Head loss in a run is the Darcy loss over the straight length PLUS the equivalent length of its fittings, L_eq = (sum L/D) x D, with sum L/D from Schedule M-601:
       h = f ((L + L_eq)/D) v^2 / (2 g)
d. The required head of a circulation set is the sum of: the static lift from the tie-in to the circuit high point (isometrics M-ISO-2xx); the head loss of the MAIN circulation path, that is the lines shown on M-601 with a single leg, at the total circuit flow; the pressure drop of every component left in the flushed path, scaled as dP_rated x (Q/Q_rated)^2 from Schedule M-602; and, for EACH skid separately at that skid's own share of the flow, the head loss of its temporary hose run and the pressure drop of its temporary strainer, scaled as dP_rated x (Q_skid/Q_rated)^2 from VD-05.
e. Where two or more skids are used on one circuit they are connected in parallel: they share the total flow equally and each must develop the required head at its own flow, per DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92.
f. A duty point beyond the last point of a published pump curve is not acceptable.
3.3   FLUSHING VELOCITY
The flushing flow of a circuit shall be not less than the flow required to achieve, in EVERY leg of EVERY line of that circuit, the greater of:
  a. the water velocity that the governing water-treatment criteria document requires for keeping foulants in suspension; and
  b. the project minimum for the circuit's velocity class, namely 4.0 ft/s for any circuit that serves a plate heat exchanger or a cold-plate device, and 2.0 ft/s otherwise.
The flushing flow shall be maintained through the initial flush, the chemical cleaning circulation and every rinse displacement.
NUMBER OF INITIAL FLUSH DISPLACEMENTS. Not fewer than ONE full circuit displacement before the cleaning charge is made up. More may be used where the Contractor judges the construction debris warrants it; the water, effluent and attended time of every displacement declared are accounted under cl.3.9 and cl.3.10 and are the Contractor's cost.
Record in the log the segment at which the velocity is lowest; that segment is the governing segment of the circuit.

Clean each circuit with the cleaning product scheduled for its metallurgy in VD-06, at the application rate stated there, referred to the SYSTEM volume of the circuit (pipework plus the hold-up of every component of the circuit, whether or not it is bypassed for flushing).
The cleaning product is dosed on that VOLUMETRIC application rate, not to a target residual: state the basis volume and the quantity of product, and leave the target residual not applicable on a cleaning row (VD-06 Note 4a).
Carry the polymer dispersant of the governing water-treatment criteria document with the cleaning charge, at the active dosage that document states for keeping foulants in suspension.
Circulate the cleaning solution for not less than the circulation time the governing water-treatment criteria document requires, then drain, flush and clean all strainers.
That circulation time is CONTACT TIME and is measured in OCCUPIED HOURS: it is the sum of the hours of the activities scheduled for the stage, and an idle gap between two of them is not contact time (cl.3.10 b).
Protect every component listed in M-602 as having a temporary bypass provision by fitting that bypass for the initial flush and the chemical cleaning. A component left in the flushed path must be shown to be within the maximum allowable pressure drop, the maximum temperature and the maximum particle size that M-602 gives it, at the declared flow.

Select the closed-system treatment program from the governing water-treatment criteria document for the circuit's metallurgy and for the makeup water analysis SW-02, and maintain the residual and pH that document specifies for the program selected.
Where that document's programme SELECTION TABLE and the controlling paragraph text of the individual programmes differ as to which programme suits a metallurgy, the paragraph text of the programme governs. The selection table is organised by system type, not by metallurgy, and does not restrict a programme to the system types it happens to list.
Where that document tabulates a quantity in more than one table, the tables it identifies for PASSIVATION govern for passivation dosages, pH bands and film-formation times; a table written for a different duty does not.
Passivate with the inhibitor technology that document tabulates for passivation, at a residual inside the tabulated dosage band and a pH inside the tabulated pH band, and hold the film-formation period that the CURRENT edition of that document tabulates.
That hold, like every other required period of this Section, is measured in OCCUPIED HOURS (cl.3.10 b).
Dose all treatment chemicals on the SYSTEM volume of the circuit.
Where copper is wetted anywhere in the circuit, carry the azole at not less than the residual the governing document requires.

[79] Where two tabulated inhibitors are carried at once - an inhibitor and a copper azole, for instance - and their tabulated pH bands overlap only in part, control to the INTERSECTION of the two bands, which satisfies both.
[80] 3.9   WATER AND EFFLUENT ACCOUNTING
[81] Account the water drawn and the effluent produced by each circuit as follows, where V_f is the circuit FLUSH volume, V_s its SYSTEM volume, n_f the number of initial flush displacements, n_r the number of rinse displacements and c is 1 if one displacement is cascaded in and 0 otherwise. State both figures for every stage in the plan.
[82]     hydrostatic test (where one is owed)   draw V_f              effluent V_f
[83]     initial flush                          draw n_f x V_f        effluent n_f x V_f
[84]     chemical cleaning                      draw V_f              effluent V_f
[85]     rinse                                  draw (n_r - c) x V_f  effluent (n_r - 1) x V_f - d
[86]     passivation charge                     draw 0                effluent 0
[87]     film-formation hold                    draw 0                effluent 0
[88]     turnover, RETAIN_AND_TOP_UP            draw V_s - V_f        effluent 0
[89]     turnover, DRAIN_AND_REFILL             draw V_s              effluent V_f
[90] The circuit is left FULL at the end of the last rinse displacement, so that displacement is not drained: that is why the rinse effluent is one displacement less than the rinse draw.
[91] The passivation charge is dosed into the water standing in the circuit at the end of the rinse; it is not a fresh fill.
[92] A rinse that takes one cascaded displacement and draws the rest from the metered supply is a single row with a single water_source: declare it CASCADE_FROM:<donor circuit>. The makeup balance above already accounts for the other displacements being drawn fresh.
[93] d is the volume this circuit DONATES to a cascade: a cascade transfers exactly one receiver displacement volume, that is the FLUSH volume of the receiving circuit, out of the donor's final rinse effluent, so the donor's effluent falls by that volume and the receiver's draw falls by the same volume. A circuit may donate to at most one receiver and receive from at most one donor, and a donor's FLUSH volume must be not less than its receiver's, or it cannot fill it.
[94] These figures balance: over the programme, water drawn equals effluent produced plus the SYSTEM volume left standing in every circuit at turnover.
[95] Water drawn by an activity that spans midnight is counted against each calendar day in proportion to the hours of the activity in that day (SW-01 cl.2).
[96] 3.10   COST BASIS
[97] Price the programme on the following basis, and report the total and its breakdown in the plan.
[98]   a. Skid rental: the fleet is on HIRE TO THE PROGRAMME, not to a circuit. Each rented unit is charged ONE day rate (SW-01 cl.3, VD-01, VD-02) for every CALENDAR DAY on which it is held anywhere on the works, counted ONCE however many circuits it serves that day. A calendar day is the period [24k, 24k+24) hours from mobilisation, k = 0, 1, 2 ... A unit is held on a day if any scheduled activity that declares it overlaps that day; a unit released for the film-formation hold is not held during it. APPORTIONMENT: divide each unit-day between the circuits that held that unit that day IN PROPORTION TO THE HOURS each held it inside the day, merging any overlap within a circuit. The share so obtained is a real number and is NOT rounded; the whole day is charged once and divided. Two circuits that share a unit-day therefore pay a part each, and a circuit whose work is spread thinly across many days pays for every one of them.
[99]   b. Commissioning crew: a crew is ENGAGED BY THE SHIFT, not by the circuit. Each crew is charged ONE shift rate for every 12-hour SHIFT [12k, 12k+12) hours from mobilisation in which it attends anything at all, counted ONCE however many circuits it attends in it. import pymupdf, numpy as np, io
from PIL import Image

def render_band(arr, r0, r1):
    sub = arr[r0:r1, :] < 160
    cols = np.where(sub.any(axis=0))[0]
    if len(cols) == 0: return ""
    c0, c1 = max(0, cols[0]-2), min(arr.shape[1], cols[-1]+3)
    sub = sub[:, c0:c1]
    # downsample horizontally by 2 if wide, or keep 1:1
    H, W = sub.shape
    lines = []
    for r in range(0, H, 2):
        row_top = sub[r]
        row_bot = sub[r+1] if r+1 < H else np.zeros_like(row_top)
        chars = []
        for t, b in zip(row_top, row_bot):
            if t and b: chars.append("█")
            elif t: chars.append("▀")
            elif b: chars.append("▄")
            else: chars.append(" ")
        lines.append("".join(chars))
    return "\n".join(lines)

doc = pymupdf.open("/filesystem/final_batch4__mechanical_task5_pcw_flush_mop__blind/site/SW-02_Municipal_Water_Analysis_Lab_Report.pdf")
im = Image.open(io.BytesIO(doc[0].extract_image(doc[0].get_images()[0][0])["image"]))
arr = np.array(im)
print(render_band(arr, 113, 146))
'

def render_braille(arr, r0, r1, c0=None, c1=None, thresh=160):
    sub = arr[r0:r1, :] < thresh
    if c0 is None or c1 is None:
        cols = np.where(sub.any(axis=0))[0]
        if len(cols) == 0: return ""
        c0, c1 = max(0, cols[0]-2), min(arr.shape[1], cols[-1]+3)
    sub = sub[:, c0:c1]
    H, W = sub.shape
    lines = []
    # braille dot mapping:
    # (0,0):1, (1,0):2, (2,0):4, (0,1):8, (1,1):16, (2,1):32, (3,0):64, (3,1):128
    dots = [(0,0,1),(1,0,2),(2,0,4),(0,1,8),(1,1,16),(2,1,32),(3,0,64),(3,1,128)]

    dark = arr < 180
    row_counts = dark.sum(axis=1)

    for r, c in enumerate(row_counts):
        if c > 3 and not in_band:

5-3.5.6 
Magnesium Silicate Scale Control. 
Formation of magnesium silicate is possible in cooling systems, but only under certain 
rare conditions. Magnesium ions (hardness) first react with hydroxyl ions (OH-) to form 
magnesium hydroxide, which then reacts with (absorbs) dissolved or colloidal silica. A 
deposit analysis often reports this material as magnesium silicate. Since magnesium 
hydroxide solubility decreases at pH levels above 9.0, this scale will usually occur only 
at a pH level above 9.0 and when the magnesium hardness concentration is greater 
than 100 ppm. 
5-3.5.7 
Silica Scale Control. 
Silica solubility is dependent upon temperature and pH. At pH levels greater than 8.5, 
silica remains soluble (no scale) at a concentration of 250 ppm as SiO2. At pH levels of 
7.5 or below, maximum silica solubility is 150 ppm as SiO2. At maximum silica levels, 
silica will first deposit on the cooling tower slats rather than in the heat exchanger 
because silica is more soluble in hot water than in cold water. The slats will become 
coated with a white, sometimes sparkling, deposit. If this occurs, blowdown should be 
increased to decrease COC by at least 1 unit. This procedure should stop additional 
scale formation. If the concentration of silica in the makeup water is above 30 ppm, it 
will usually be the parameter that controls the adjustment of cooling water system COC. 
If the silica concentration is high, external treatment can reduce the level of silica in the 
makeup water (see Chapter 3). The introduction of water treatment chemicals based on 
new polymer technology may allow the solubility of silica to be increased above the old 
recognized limit of 150 ppm.

5-3.6 
Cooling Water Fouling. 
The term “fouling” refers to the deposition of materials that are normally held in 
suspension in the cooling water: mud, silt, and other SS brought into the system with 
the makeup water; dust, dirt, and debris scrubbed out of the air passing through the 
tower; product leakage such as oils; corrosion products from the system; and biological 
organisms, both living and dead. Combinations of any or all of these materials can be 
present in the cooling water. 
5-3.7 
Fouling Control. 
Fouling from mud, dirt, and corrosion products can be controlled by the addition of a 
water-soluble polymer dispersant, such as a polyacrylate. The addition of about 4 to 5 
ppm of active polymer, together with sufficient water velocity (3.28 feet per second (1 
meter per second)), can keep foulants in suspension and prevent them from being 
deposited on heat transfer surfaces. Higher dosages (5 to 20 ppm) of active polymer 
can be required for heavily fouled systems. It is best to reduce the loading of SS by 
mechanically removing them from the system through blowdown, filtration, and physical 
sump cleaning. Removing oil or oily materials requires a non-foaming surfactant. 
Paragraph 5-4 describes prevention of fouling by biological organisms. Table 5-2 
summarizes foulant control methods.

5-4 
MICROBIOLOGICAL DEPOSITS AND CONTROL. 
Microbiological organisms are composed of three classes: algae, bacteria, and fungus. 
Large biological organisms such as clams, snails, mussels, or similar species are 
referred to as macrobiological organisms. The presence of any biological growth can be 
detrimental to cooling tower operations. Problems include fouling, corrosion, and loss of 
efficiency. 
These problems can lead to downtime, higher operating cost, and even premature 
replacement of equipment. Additionally, some bacteria are pathogenic and can pose a 
risk to human life. 
5-4.1 
Algae. 
The term “algae” refers to algal, microbiological, tiny, stringy blue and blue-green plants, 
which are usually found growing in masses on top of and on sides of cooling towers. 


==================== PAGE 145 ====================

123 
Algae grow only in sunlit areas. They will slough off and become part of the suspended 
matter in the circulating water, a situation which may cause fouling and plugging of 
water sprays. Algae also provide a breeding place, and are a nutrient, for bacteria. 
5-4.2 
Bacteria. 
The term “bacteria” refers to a large group of one-celled microorganisms. Bacteria can 
grow in either the absence or presence of sunlight. There are several ways to classify 
bacteria, including “aerobic,” meaning those living in the presence of oxygen, and 
“anaerobic,” meaning those living in the absence of oxygen. In a cooling water system, 
one can categorize bacteria as either “planktonic” or “sessile,” which are terms that 
describe whether the bacteria are, respectively, either free floating or found growing on 
surfaces (stickers). Categories of bacteria are described below. Table 5-3 shows types 
of bacteria and their growth conditions. 
5-4.2.1 
Planktonic Bacteria. 
Planktonic bacteria are suspended in the water, sometimes referred to as “free floaters” 
or “swimmers,” and are aerobic bacteria that thrive in an oxygenated environment. They 
are not harmful to the cooling system since they do not cause deposits or corrosion, but 
they can provide nutrients for other microorganisms; in addition, some planktonic 
bacteria such as Legionella Pneumophila are pathogenic and can present a significant 
human health risk. 
5-4.2.2 
Sessile Bacteria. 
Sessile bacteria are stickers, or non-swimming bacteria, and can cause deposits and 
corrosion. Sessile bacteria types include slime-formers and anaerobic (corrosive) 
bacteria. Slime-formers can grow and form gelatinous deposits on almost any surface in 
contact with the cooling water. These deposits can grow so large that they restrict water 
flow and interfere with heat transfer; they also may promote under-deposit corrosion. 
Feeling the sides of the cooling tower basin just below the water level is one way to 
detect the presence of slime-formers. Usually if there are slime formers in the system, 
you can feel deposits. Anaerobic bacteria thrive in oxygen- deprived environments and 
often establish colonies beneath slime deposits or under other types of deposits. One 
type of anaerobe is sulfate-reducing bacteria (SRB), which produce hydrogen sulfide, a 
chemical that is very corrosive to metals. This type of corrosion attack is much localized 
and can result in pipe and tube failures. The presence of SRB should be suspected in a 
water system if the underside of a slime layer is black or if you detect the odor of rotten 
eggs. Any type of microbiological corrosion is referred to as microbiologically influenced 
corrosion (MIC). Bacteria cause most of the MIC found in cooling water systems. Use 
surface microbiological measurements to monitor sessile bacteria.

The term “fungi” refers to classes of organisms made up of molds and yeasts, some of

special preservative treatment of wood. Fungi also produce deposits in cooling water

Microbiological Control. 
The term “microbiological control” refers to techniques used to minimize the presence of 
microbiological organisms in cooling water. Chemical biocide treatment is the method 
used on government installations for microbiological control in cooling water. Biocides 
that are used to control microbiological growth fall into one of two broad categories: 
oxidizing and non-oxidizing microbiocides. A cost-effective approach for control involves 
the regular use of oxidizers as a primary biocide, augmented by selective use of non-
oxidizing biocides. Important factors for the effectiveness of any biocide include using a 
proper dosage and allowing adequate contact time with the microbiological organisms. 
All microbiocides are toxic and must be handled safely and with caution; use the SDS 
for safety instructions.

5-5.5.1 
Effective Corrosion Control. 
Effective corrosion control requires maintaining appropriate pH levels, plus adding 
maintenance dosages of chemical corrosion inhibitors. Chemical corrosion inhibitors 
form a protective film or barrier on the cooling system metal surfaces that have been 
cleaned prior to adding an initial high dosage of inhibitor. The initial high dosage of 
inhibitor passivates (protects) the metal. The appropriate dosage of corrosion inhibitor 
must be maintained continuously in the cooling water to ensure continuing protection. 
Table 5-11 shows examples of various passivation and maintenance dosage levels of 
corrosion inhibitors. Corrosion inhibitors are divided into three classes: cathodic, anodic, 
and general filmers. Corrosion inhibitors form a protective film on either the anode, the 
cathode, or over the entire metal surface. The types of corrosion inhibitors are 
described below. 
5-5.5.1.1 
Anodic Inhibitors. 
Anodic inhibitors form a protective film coating on the anodic metal (where the metal is 
lost) and thus directly control corrosion by preventing the reaction that results in 
corrosion. Any unprotected areas will corrode at a much faster rate than the protected 
areas, a factor that could result in pitting or localized attack of the unprotected areas. 
Examples of anodic inhibitors include orthophosphate, nitrite, and orthosilicates. Under 
certain conditions, molybdate can function as an anodic inhibitor. 


==================== PAGE 160 ====================

1 March 2023 
 
138 
5-5.5.1.2 
Cathodic Inhibitors. 
Cathodic inhibitors form a protective film coating of the cathodic metal (where metal is 
not lost) and thus indirectly prevent corrosion by interfering with the current flow 
required for the electrochemical reaction to proceed between the cathodic and anodic 
metals. The corrosion reaction rate is governed by the size and type of the cathode 
relative to the anode. Even when cathodic areas are not completely covered by the 
protective film, corrosion will occur, but usually more slowly and uniformly than when 
using anodic inhibitors alone. The occurrence of localized corrosion or pitting attack is 
greatly reduced. Examples of cathodic inhibitors include zinc salts, polyphosphates, and 
polysilicates. Under most conditions, molybdate will function as a cathodic inhibitor. 
5-5.5.1.3 
General Inhibitors. 
General inhibitors produce a protective film on the surfaces of all metals. These 
corrosion inhibitors are organic compounds, such as certain phosphonates, amines, and 
other nitrogen chemicals. They may be used in cooling water systems. 
5-5.5.1.4 
Corrosion Inhibitors for Specific Metals. 
Some corrosion inhibitors provide corrosion control for specific metals. The protection of 
copper and copper alloys requires the use of azoles, such as tolyltriazole (TTA), 
benzotriazole (BZT), and butylbenzo-thiazole, which can be added to the system 
separately from, or as part of a blend of, other treatment chemicals. 
5-5.5.1.5 
Galvanic or Crevice Corrosion. 
Control of galvanic or crevice corrosion is achieved primarily by engineering and 
mechanical design. These types of corrosion can also be partially controlled by physical 
and chemical considerations. A dielectric coupling (insulator), used to separate two 
different metallurgies, can help to prevent galvanic corrosion. From a chemical 
perspective, adjusting pH and using proper corrosion inhibitors will reduce corrosion. 
5-5.5.1.6 
Deposit Corrosion. 
Control of deposit corrosion requires maintaining deposit-free metal surfaces. This 
applies to any form of deposit, such as scale, biomass, corrosion products, or foulants. 
The occurrence of most types of deposits is prevented by dispersants, scale inhibitors, 
or biocides, along with the maintenance of adequate flow velocities. Routine, adequate 
cleaning of filters and tower sumps will help reduce deposits. 
5-5.5.1.7 
MIC. 
MIC is best prevented by stopping conditions that foster biological growth and by using 
an effective microbiological control program. A MIC prevention program includes 
adequate control (prevention) of deposits and fouling, avoidance of low-flow and dead-
leg conditions, and implementation of a consistently effective microbiological program 
(see paragraph 5-4.4).

PROGRAM. 
An effective and complete cooling water treatment program addresses many factors, 
including those associated with compliance and safety, protection of equipment, and 
cost. Compliance and safety considerations are mandatory components of the program. 
Achieving or exceeding minimally acceptable equipment protection at the lowest 
possible cost is an advisable outcome for a well-designed program. The overall cost of 
the treatment program includes not only the cost of chemical treatment, but also the 
costs of water, disposal, manpower, and equipment. Development of an appropriate 
cooling water treatment program is dependent upon knowledge of both the specific 
equipment to be protected and the quality of the water to be used (source water and 
system water). 
5-6.1

Corrosion inhibitors are selected based on the metallurgy of individual pieces of cooling 
system equipment. Typical systems include equipment components of different metals.

Operational features and parameters of the cooling water system must be known to 
select the proper scale and deposit inhibitors. This requirement refers to operational 
parameters such as maximum temperature, minimum velocities, usage patterns, and 
whether or not layup periods occur. The best chemical treatment programs cannot 
overcome the stresses of poorly operated systems. A good example of system stress is 
intermittent chiller operation that allows for SS accumulation (deposits) in chiller tube 
surfaces due to low flow or lack of flow. This situation creates a strong potential for 
under-deposit corrosion and for MIC that the chemical treatment may not be able to 
overcome completely. Stagnant water can also cause deposits and corrosion. High 
water temperatures can cause scale. The maximum water temperature should be 
known so that the proper scale-control method can be used.

Water quality within the cooling water system is a critical consideration. The source may

appropriate water treatment chemicals can be selected for controlling specific water 
quality parameters.

Small-sized towers – capacity less than 25 tons (88 kilowatts)

cost. Compliance and safety considerations are mandatory components of the program. 
Achieving or exceeding minimally acceptable equipment protection at the lowest 
possible cost is an advisable outcome for a well-designed program. The overall cost of 
the treatment program includes not only the cost of chemical treatment, but also the 
costs of water, disposal, manpower, and equipment. Development of an appropriate 
cooling water treatment program is dependent upon knowledge of both the specific 
equipment to be protected and the quality of the water to be used (source water and 
system water). 
5-6.1 
Equipment. 
Corrosion inhibitors are selected based on the metallurgy of individual pieces of cooling 
system equipment. Typical systems include equipment components of different metals. 
For example, systems may include smooth and enhanced copper tube bundles, mild 
steel transfer piping, and galvanized cooling tower components; therefore, to select the

6-1.1.2 
Description of Hot Water Systems. 
A typical hot water (hydronic) heating system is similar in composition to the closed 
cooling water system shown in Figure 6-2, except that a fired or non-fired heat 
exchanger is used rather than a chiller. Hot water boilers (fired and unfired) differ from 
steam boilers described in Chapter 4 because hot water boilers: 
• 
Provide heated water but do not generate steam. 
• 
Do not have deaerating heaters. (These are not required because there is 
essentially no makeup water requirement and thus very little air enters the 
system.) 
• 
Require recirculating pumps to distribute the heated water to the 
processing equipment. 
• 
Require expansion tanks that contain a cushion of steam or nitrogen. 
• 
Do not contain a condensate return because there is no steam generated, 
but there is a return system. 
• 
Do not require blowdown. 
• 
Are fabricated with mild steel components, but also may contain copper 
heat exchanger tubes, particularly in unfired systems.

6-1.2 
Closed Chilled Water Systems, Brine Systems, and Glycol Systems. 
Closed chilled water systems, brine systems, and glycol systems supply cold or chilled 
water for cooling processes and air conditioning. They are water systems designed for 
minimal loss of water. These systems contain mild steel piping, copper heat exchangers 
and, in some systems, aluminum piping, stainless steel piping, cold rolled steel piping, 
and potentially other metals. 
6-1.2.1 
Closed Chilled Water Systems. 
Closed chilled water systems circulate water that is cooled by refrigeration equipment. 
Water temperature ranges typically vary between 40 to 55° F (4 to 13° C). A typical 
chilled water system is depicted in Figure 6-2. Chilled water systems can have large 
storage capacity (1,000,000 gallons (3785 cubic meters) or higher). Chillers are shown 
in Figure 6-3.

6-1.2.2 
Closed Brine Systems. 
Closed brine systems are chilled water systems in which calcium chloride, sodium 
chloride, or a mixture of sodium chloride and calcium chloride has been added to the 
water to lower its freezing point sufficiently to maintain it as a liquid (ice-free) at 
temperatures of 30 to 50° F (-1 to 10° C). Brine systems have been largely replaced by 
glycol systems. 
6-1.2.3 
Closed Glycol Systems. 
Closed glycol systems are chilled water systems that contain a mixture of water and 
glycol (ethylene or propylene) that will not freeze at the system operating temperature of 
20 to 35° F (-7 to 2° C). 
6-1.3 
Combined Hot and Chilled Water Systems. 
Some closed systems serve the dual purpose of producing circulating hot water during 
the cold season and chilled water during the hot season. 
6-1.4 
Diesel Engine Jacket Cooling Systems. 
Diesel engine cooling systems are considered closed systems, even when surge tanks 
are open to the atmosphere. 
The heat transfer from the circulating water is usually accomplished using a heat 
exchanger, not by evaporation. These systems have low water losses. Several of the 
metals used in these systems require good corrosion control. The three basic types of 
diesel engine cooling systems are described below.

6-1.4.1 
Air-Cooled Diesel Cooling Systems. 
Air-cooled diesel cooling systems are used on most small engines as well as some large 
engines. The jacket water is circulated through an air-cooled radiator. Antifreeze must 
be used in these systems when radiators are exposed to low-temperature atmospheric 
air or when the water temperature exceeds the boiling point (212° F (100° C)) 
6-1.4.2 
Water-Cooled Diesel Engine Cooling Systems. 
Water-cooled diesel engine cooling systems are used mainly on large engines. The 
jacket cooling water passes through a heat exchanger, rather than a radiator, where a 
separate cooling water loop removes the heat from the jacket cooling water. These 
systems commonly use antifreeze. 
6-1.4.3 
Vapor-Phase Diesel Engine Cooling Systems. 
Vapor-phase diesel engine cooling systems, also called ebullient systems, use water 
that is heated to a temperature at the boiling point or above the boiling point for 
pressurized systems. Steam is formed from the cooling water as it removes heat from 
the system. The steam produced in this way can be recovered and used for space 
heating. This type of system requires significant amounts of makeup water and 
chemical treatment. 
6-2 
WATER TREATMENT FOR CLOSED SYSTEMS. 
Water treatment programs for both closed hot water and closed chilled water systems 
are developed primarily to control corrosion, although the programs may also control 
deposition and microbiological organisms. If needed, scale deposition can be prevented 
by external treatment (as with ion exchange softening) or can be controlled with 
inhibitors as described in Chapter 4. Corrosion must be completely controlled by water 
treatment programs. If corrosion occurs, corrosion products will eventually plug the 
system, resulting in decreased operational efficiency and the need for cleaning. 
Microbiological growth is not a concern in hot water systems, but can occur in chilled 
water systems and should be controlled (see paragraph 6-2.3). 
6-2.1 
Makeup Water Requirements. 
Makeup water requirements for closed systems are very small unless there are leaks in 
the system (see paragraph 6-2.4). Closed systems should not be drained or purged 
unless there is evidence that indicates the need to remove dirty water or sludge. For 
proper operation, makeup water in high- temperature and medium-temperature water 
systems is deaerated (de-oxygenated) using both mechanical and chemical methods 
and is also softened. Oxygen can be removed from low-temperature water systems 
either chemically or mechanically to prevent oxygen-induced corrosion. Chilled water 
systems can require partial softening if the makeup water exceeds 250 ppm total 
hardness (as CaCO3). The makeup water requirements are monitored carefully in 
systems of all types (see Table 6-1). If there is an increase in the quantity of makeup

Identifying Water Leaks. 
The best way to check for leaks in a closed water system is to periodically read and 
record the water usage displayed by a totalizing water meter installed in the makeup 
water line or to use an inert, fluorescent material indicate a leak. The florescent material 
can also be used to help pinpoint leaks or do leak studies. If the system does not have a 
water meter, the existence of leaks can be checked by testing the inhibitor 
concentration in the circulating water. The inhibitor concentration should be measured

its concentration has decreased while the conductivity has remained constant, biological 
contamination is present. If the measured values for both parameters decrease, there is

sample that is a mixture of influent and effluent water on ion exchange units that use 
automatic regeneration and multi-port valves.

measure its strength. The sodium chloride brine should be as near 100 percent 
saturation as possible (approximately 28 percent by weight) for efficient softener 
regeneration.

Routine and appropriate testing of the system water is an essential component of a 
water treatment program. Water testing provides information that can be used: to 
ensure the protection of the water system equipment; to prevent unexpected system 
failure; to provide information used to control water quality; and to verify that water 
treatment chemicals are maintained at the proper concentrations within the system or, if 
not, to allow for adjustment of their concentrations. An adequate testing program

reasons. This determination can involve reanalysis and checking of the test reagents. If 
the test results are correct, the water quality and water treatment program must be re-
evaluated and modified, if necessary. Paragraph 7-6 describes interpretation of water 
test results.

5-1.4.2 
Water-Cooled Diesel Engine Cooling Systems. Water-cooled diesel 
engine cooling systems are used mainly on large engines. The jacket cooling water 
passes through a heat exchanger, rather than a radiator, where a separate cooling 
water loop removes the heat from the jacket cooling water. These systems commonly 
use antifreeze. 
 
5-1.4.3 
Vapor-Phase Diesel Engine Cooling Systems. Vapor-phase diesel 
engine cooling systems, also called ebullient systems, use water that is heated to a 
temperature at the boiling point or above the boiling point for pressurized systems. 
Steam is formed from the cooling water as it removes heat from the system. The steam 
produced in this way can be recovered and used for space heating. This type of system 
requires significant amounts of makeup water and chemical treatment. 
 
5-2 
WATER TREATMENT FOR CLOSED SYSTEMS. Water treatment 
programs for both closed hot water and closed chilled water systems are developed 
primarily to control corrosion, although the programs may also control deposition and 
microbiological organisms. If needed, scale deposition can be prevented by external 
treatment (i.e., ion exchange softening) or can be controlled with inhibitors as described 
in Chapter 4. Corrosion must be completely controlled by water treatment programs. If 
corrosion occurs, corrosion products will eventually plug the system, resulting in 
decreased operational efficiency and the need for cleaning. Microbiological growth is not 
a concern in hot water systems, but can occur in chilled water systems and should be 
controlled (see paragraph 5-2.3). 
 
5-2.1 
Makeup Water Requirements. Makeup water requirements for closed 
systems are very small unless there are leaks in the system (see paragraph 5-2.4).  
Closed systems should not be drained or purged unless there is evidence that indicates 
the need to remove dirty water or sludge. For proper operation, makeup water in high-
temperature and medium-temperature water systems is deaerated (de-oxygenated) 
using both mechanical and chemical methods and is also softened. Oxygen can be 
removed from low-temperature water systems either chemically or mechanically to 
prevent oxygen-induced corrosion. Chilled water systems can require partial softening if 
the makeup water exceeds 250 ppm total hardness (as CaCO ). The makeup water 
requirements are monitored carefully in systems of all types (see Table 5-1).  If there is 
an increase in the quantity of makeup water required, the leak should be found and 
repaired quickly. After the repair, water treatment chemicals should be replenished 
immediately.

Treatment and Control of Microbiological Growth. Treatment and 
control of microbiological growth is a concern in chilled or closed cooling water systems. 
It is a particular concern if a nitrite-based corrosion inhibitor is used. Nitrite can serve as

not be used since they are not compatible with nitrite water treatment. 
 
5-2.4 
Identifying Water Leaks. The best way to check for leaks in a closed 
water system is to periodically read and record the water usage displayed by a totalizing 
water meter installed in the makeup water line or to use an inert, fluorescent material 
indicate a leak.  The florescent material can also be used to help pinpoint leaks or do 
leak studies. If the system does not have a water meter, the existence of leaks can be 
checked by testing the inhibitor concentration in the circulating water.  The inhibitor 
concentration should be measured once per month using molybdate, polysilicate, or 
azole, but not nitrite. Do not depend upon the nitrite test; nitrite can be lost due to 
bacteria action. If nitrite is measured and its concentration has decreased while the 
conductivity has remained constant, biological contamination is present. If the measured 
values for both parameters decrease, there is a leak in the system. Borate 
concentration would be the best indicator of leak detection.  When the inhibitor 
concentration has dropped to 98% of the original value, about 2% of the system water 
will have been lost. If the lapsed time for this 2% loss is less than 4 months, the 
system's loss of water is excessive and any leaks should be found and eliminated. 
Another convenient indication of water loss is the measurement over time of a drop in 
conductivity. If the system water conductivity equals that of the makeup, the treatment 
chemical is totally absent.  Inert florescent material can be added to the system and 
used to help pinpoint leaks, or do leak studies.  Loss of the fluorescent material can be 
monitored in real time; such loss indicates a leak. 
 
NOTE: A 2% loss over 4 months equals 0.5% loss per month. The accuracy of this test 
is limited, so if the loss for any month exceeds 1%, the test should be repeated. If 
retesting confirms the water loss, the leaks should be found and eliminated.

LAMINAR AND TURBULENT FLOW
Average (Bulk) Velocity
In many fluid flow problems, instead of determining exact velocities at different locations in the
same flow cross-section, it is sufficient to allow a single average velocity to represent the
velocity of all fluid at that point in the pipe. This is fairly simple for turbulent flow since the
velocity profile is flat over the majority of the pipe cross-section. It is reasonable to assume that
the average velocity is the same as the velocity at the center of the pipe.
If the flow regime is laminar (the velocity profile is parabolic), the problem still exists of trying
to represent the "average" velocity at any given cross-section since an average value is used in
the fluid flow equations. Technically, this is done by means of integral calculus. Practically, the
student should use an average value that is half of the center line value.
Viscosity
Viscosity is a fluid property that measures the resistance of the fluid to deforming due to a shear
force.
Viscosity is the internal friction of a fluid which makes it resist flowing past a solid
surface or other layers of the fluid. Viscosity can also be considered to be a measure of the
resistance of a fluid to flowing. A thick oil has a high viscosity; water has a low viscosity. The
unit of measurement for absolute viscosity is:
µ = absolute viscosity of fluid (lbf-sec/ft2).
The viscosity of a fluid is usually significantly dependent on the temperature of the fluid and
relatively independent of the pressure. For most fluids, as the temperature of the fluid increases,
the viscosity of the fluid decreases. An example of this can be seen in the lubricating oil of
engines. When the engine and its lubricating oil are cold, the oil is very viscous, or thick. After
the engine is started and the lubricating oil increases in temperature, the viscosity of the oil
decreases significantly and the oil seems much thinner.
Ideal Fluid
An ideal fluid is one that is incompressible and has no viscosity. Ideal fluids do not actually
exist, but sometimes it is useful to consider what would happen to an ideal fluid in a particular
fluid flow problem in order to simplify the problem.
Reynolds Number
The flow regime (either laminar or turbulent) is determined by evaluating the Reynolds number
of the flow (refer to figure 5). The Reynolds number, based on studies of Osborn Reynolds, is
a dimensionless number comprised of the physical characteristics of the flow. Equation 3-7 is
used to calculate the Reynolds number (NR) for fluid flow.

an example of which is shown in Appendix B. Additional detail on the use of the Moody Chart

Summary
The main points of this chapter are summarized below.
Laminar and Turbulent Flow Summary
•
Laminar Flow
Layers of water flow over one another at different speeds with virtually no
mixing between layers.
The flow velocity profile for laminar flow in circular pipes is parabolic in shape,
with a maximum flow in the center of the pipe and a minimum flow at the pipe
walls.
The average flow velocity is approximately one half of the maximum velocity.
•
Turbulent Flow
The flow is characterized by the irregular movement of particles of the fluid.
The flow velocity profile for turbulent flow is fairly flat across the center section
of a pipe and drops rapidly extremely close to the walls.
The average flow velocity is approximately equal to the velocity at the center of
the pipe.
•
Viscosity is the fluid property that measures the resistance of the fluid to deforming
due to a shear force.
For most fluids, temperature and viscosity are inversely
proportional.
•
An ideal fluid is one that is incompressible and has no viscosity.
•
An increasing Reynolds number indicates an increasing turbulence of flow.

Head Loss
Head loss is a measure of the reduction in the total head (sum of elevation head, velocity head
and pressure head) of the fluid as it moves through a fluid system. Head loss is unavoidable in
real fluids. It is present because of: the friction between the fluid and the walls of the pipe; the
friction between adjacent fluid particles as they move relative to one another; and the turbulence
caused whenever the flow is redirected or affected in any way by such components as piping
entrances and exits, pumps, valves, flow reducers, and fittings.
Frictional loss is that part of the total head loss that occurs as the fluid flows through straight
pipes. The head loss for fluid flow is directly proportional to the length of pipe, the square of
the fluid velocity, and a term accounting for fluid friction called the friction factor. The head
loss is inversely proportional to the diameter of the pipe.

For practical purposes, if the Reynolds number is less than 2000, the flow is laminar. If it is
greater than 3500, the flow is turbulent. Flows with Reynolds numbers between 2000 and 3500
are sometimes referred to as transitional flows. Most fluid systems in nuclear facilities operate
with turbulent flow. Reynolds numbers can be conveniently determined using a Moody Chart;
an example of which is shown in Appendix B. Additional detail on the use of the Moody Chart
is provided in subsequent text.
Summary
The main points of this chapter are summarized below.
Laminar and Turbulent Flow Summary
•
Laminar Flow
Layers of water flow over one another at different speeds with virtually no
mixing between layers.
The flow velocity profile for laminar flow in circular pipes is parabolic in shape,
with a maximum flow in the center of the pipe and a minimum flow at the pipe
walls.
The average flow velocity is approximately one half of the maximum velocity.
•
Turbulent Flow
The flow is characterized by the irregular movement of particles of the fluid.
The flow velocity profile for turbulent flow is fairly flat across the center section
of a pipe and drops rapidly extremely close to the walls.
The average flow velocity is approximately equal to the velocity at the center of
the pipe.
•
Viscosity is the fluid property that measures the resistance of the fluid to deforming
due to a shear force.
For most fluids, temperature and viscosity are inversely
proportional.
•
An ideal fluid is one that is incompressible and has no viscosity.
•
An increasing Reynolds number indicates an increasing turbulence of flow.

Head Loss
Head loss is a measure of the reduction in the total head (sum of elevation head, velocity head
and pressure head) of the fluid as it moves through a fluid system. Head loss is unavoidable in
real fluids. It is present because of: the friction between the fluid and the walls of the pipe; the
friction between adjacent fluid particles as they move relative to one another; and the turbulence
caused whenever the flow is redirected or affected in any way by such components as piping
entrances and exits, pumps, valves, flow reducers, and fittings.
Frictional loss is that part of the total head loss that occurs as the fluid flows through straight
pipes. The head loss for fluid flow is directly proportional to the length of pipe, the square of
the fluid velocity, and a term accounting for fluid friction called the friction factor. The head
loss is inversely proportional to the diameter of the pipe.

System Use of Multiple Centrifugal Pumps
A typical centrifugal pump has a relatively low number of moving parts and can be easily
adapted to a variety of prime movers. These prime movers include AC and DC electric motors,
diesel engines, steam turbines, and air motors. Centrifugal pumps are typically small in size and
can usually be built for a relatively low cost.
In addition, centrifugal pumps provide a high
volumetric flow rate with a relatively low pressure.
In order to increase the volumetric flow rate in a system or to compensate for large flow
resistances, centrifugal pumps are often used in parallel or in series.
Figure 11 depicts two
identical centrifugal pumps operating at the same speed in parallel.

system, each pump must produce the same pump head.
